doc.title: Tom Varner interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 13, 2025

chapter: Writing for horn, politics and creativity
title: Horn and saxophone unisons and playing tough lines again
summary: The horn blends differently than trumpet with sax, per Jim McNeely 'glue'; he and Ed Jackson relearned his hard tune on the sabbatical.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: One thing that I think is wonderful about your tunes is that when you write unison lines with the horn, whether it’s with alto or tenor sax – they sound so different from if you
were playing the trumpet. We’re so used to that trumpet-sax – you know, all through bebop – and the tone quality of the horn just makes it like a new thing.

Yeah. Yeah. It’s true. I used to talk about that with the arranger/composer Jim McNeely, that he would say, “The horn is kind of like this glue. If it’s a larger ensemble and there’s a horn inside there you might not hear, like, ‘Oh there’s a French horn in there.’ But if you take away the horn you’re going, ‘Oh that’s totally different.’” It provides this – well he used the word “glue” between the different instruments. And it’s true. The overtones of the sax and the overtones of the French horn are such that when they’re together it’s very different from trumpet and sax, or two saxes or two horns for that matter. So I’ve always loved that.

Some of those tougher lines that you’ve written I almost wondered like you were writing them knowing that a really good sax player could play them, and then you almost forgot that you had to play it too.

Yeah. You got it. That’s true sometimes. Or you could play it when you’re 28 and then you’re going to revisit it when you’re 58 and you’re like what was I thinking – how am I going to play that? And that one called “What is This Thing Called First Strike Capability” on this sabbatical, it was wonderful. I met up with Ed Jackson, the alto player again, and we played in this club that he has a small kind of informal club which is wonderful near Elmont in Queens, Jamaica Queens. And we played that tune and I was like whoa, we got together and we both had to practice that one again. And he also was saying there’s a section in the bridge [scats] it’s the worst because it’s the pinky. As an alto sax player you have to do this pinky. I didn’t know. For me, that part of it was actually easy. And all sax players were like, “Why did you pick those three notes?” Sorry. I’ll let the sax players do a little work on that one.
Really. They’ve got all those keys. It should be easy.
